sections.title: What This Module Covers
sections.body: This module introduces software design principles relevant to entry-level Rails developers. You will learn: the five SOLID principles at a conceptual level (Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, Dependency Inversion), the DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) principle and how to apply it in Ruby with methods, modules, and concerns, service objects as a pattern for extracting business logic out of fat controllers and models, and simple design patterns that appear in Rails code (the Decorator pattern, the Query Object pattern, and the Presenter pattern).

sections.title: Key Concepts at a Glance
sections.body: SOLID: S — Single Responsibility: a class should have one reason to change. O — Open/Closed: open for extension, closed for modification (use inheritance/modules). L — Liskov Substitution: subclasses should be substitutable for their parent class. I — Interface Segregation: don't force classes to depend on methods they don't use. D — Dependency Inversion: depend on abstractions, not concretions (inject dependencies). DRY: every piece of knowledge should have a single representation. Extract repeated logic into methods. Use modules/concerns to share code across models. Rails concerns in app/models/concerns/ and app/controllers/concerns/. Service Objects: Plain Ruby classes in app/services/. One public method (call or perform). Example: UserRegistrationService.new(params).call. Keep models and controllers thin. Simple patterns: Decorator wraps an object to add behaviour. Query Object encapsulates a complex ActiveRecord query. Presenter (or Decorator via Draper gem) for view-specific formatting.

sections.title: What Interviewers Ask Freshers
sections.body: Key design fresher questions: (1) What is the Single Responsibility Principle? Give a Rails example. (2) What does DRY mean and how do you apply it? (3) What is a service object and why would you use one? (4) What is the difference between a fat model and a skinny controller? (5) What is a Rails concern and when would you use it? (6) What is the Decorator pattern? (7) How would you refactor a controller action that is doing too much? (8) What is Dependency Injection? (9) Why is it a bad idea to put all your business logic in the controller? (10) What is the difference between a module (mixin) and a service object for sharing code? These questions test whether you are thinking about code quality, not just making things work.
